topics.title: Humorous poems: rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration

learn.hook: Can a paratha be used as a brick? In a funny poem, anything can happen!
points: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words and their meanings.
Rhyme: words that end with the same sound, like thick and brick. A rhyme scheme labels line endings with letters: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme; ABAB means lines 1-3 and 2-4 rhyme.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem, made by the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. A bouncy rhythm makes a funny poem fun to read aloud.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect: 'I've told you a million times!'
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash). Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words (Bunty bought big balloons).

example.q: Read this original poem: 'Our cook made parathas so heavy and thick, / Our dog used one as a brand-new brick. / Papa took a bite and his jaw went CRACK! / Now he wants his teeth and his money back!' Think it through: what is the rhyme scheme, and where is the exaggeration?
steps: Line endings: thick (A), brick (A), crack (B), back (B).
So the rhyme scheme is AABB.
No real paratha could be used as a brick: that is hyperbole.
'CRACK' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia that adds to the fun.
example.answer: The rhyme scheme is AABB, and the paratha-as-a-brick line is hyperbole.

learn.reallife: Advertising jingles, cricket chants and birthday rhymes use rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration to stick in your memory.

games.title: Name the trick
items: I've told you a million times!
I'm so hungry I could eat an elephant.
The kettle hissed on the stove.

quiz.q: Read: 'Our cook made parathas so heavy and thick, / Our dog used one as a brand-new brick.' Which two words rhyme?
quiz.explain: Rhyming words end with the same sound: thick and brick both end in '-ick'.
steps: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
The line-endings 'thick' and 'brick' both end in '-ick'.
Answer: thick, brick
quiz.mistake: Looks for words that share letters at the start instead of sounds at the end

quiz.q: A four-line stanza has lines 1 and 2 rhyming and lines 3 and 4 rhyming. What is its rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: The first two lines share sound A, the next two share sound B: AABB.
steps: Lines 1 and 2 share one sound (A); lines 3 and 4 share another (B).
So the rhyme scheme is AABB.
Answer: AABB
quiz.mistake: Mixes up couplets (AABB) with alternate rhyme (ABAB)

quiz.q: Read: 'Papa took a bite and his jaw went CRACK!' The word 'CRACK' is an example of ___.
quiz.explain: 'Crack' imitates the sound it names, which is onomatopoeia.
steps: 'CRACK' imitates the sound it names.
A word that imitates a sound is onomatopoeia.
Answer: onomatopoeia
quiz.mistake: Thinks any figure of speech in a poem is a simile or metaphor

options: Our dog used the paratha as a brand-new brick.
quiz.explain: A paratha cannot really be used as a brick. This deliberate exaggeration is hyperbole.
steps: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration.
A paratha cannot really be used as a brick, so that line is hyperbole.
Answer: Our dog used the paratha as a brand-new brick.
quiz.mistake: Does not separate an ordinary description from an exaggeration

options: I like to read at night.
Peter's pet parrot plays the piano.
The rain fell on the roof.
quiz.explain: The 'p' sound repeats at the start of Peter's, pet, parrot, plays and piano.
steps: Alliteration repeats the same first sound in nearby words.
'Peter's pet parrot plays the piano' repeats 'p'.
Answer: Peter's pet parrot plays the piano.
quiz.mistake: Thinks alliteration means rhyme at the end of lines

options: A word that imitates a sound
A word with the same meaning
quiz.explain: Hyperbole means exaggerating on purpose, often to be funny or to stress a point.
steps: Hyperbole means exaggerating on purpose.
A comparison with like/as is a simile; a sound word is onomatopoeia.
Answer: A deliberate exaggeration
quiz.mistake: Confuses hyperbole with simile or onomatopoeia

quiz.explain: 'Laugh' and 'half' end with the same sound '-af', even though they are spelt differently.
steps: Rhyme depends on sound, not spelling.
'Laugh' and 'half' both end with the sound '-af'.
Answer: half
quiz.mistake: Matches the first letter or the spelling instead of the ending sound

quiz.q: In the rhyme scheme ABAB, which lines rhyme?
quiz.explain: The letter A marks lines 1 and 3; the letter B marks lines 2 and 4. Lines with the same letter rhyme.
steps: Lines with the same letter rhyme.
In ABAB, A = lines 1 and 3, B = lines 2 and 4.
Answer: Lines 1 and 3, lines 2 and 4
quiz.mistake: Reads ABAB as pairs of neighbouring lines

teach.ask: Gappu giggles: Why is a poem about a paratha used as a brick so funny? What tricks does the poet use?
teach.praise: Ha! Big exaggeration, bouncy rhymes and sound words like CRACK. That is why funny poems are fun!
teach.nudge: Could a paratha really be a brick? What do we call that? And what do the line endings do?

revise.summary: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words. We learn rhyme, rhyme scheme, rhythm, hyperbole, onomatopoeia and alliteration.
focus: Find rhyming words by their ending sound.
Work out AABB and ABAB rhyme schemes.
remember: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme; ABAB means lines 1-3 and 2-4 rhyme.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Onomatopoeia imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash); alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words.
traps: Rhyme is about the ending sound, not the spelling or first letter: 'laugh' rhymes with 'half'.
Don't read ABAB as pairs of neighbouring lines.
Alliteration is not rhyme at the end of lines.

topics.title: Fun with language: puns, homophones and homonyms

learn.hook: Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school! Words with two meanings make the best jokes.
points: A pun is a joke that plays on a word with two meanings, or on two words that sound alike.
The title 'A Concrete Example' can be read two ways: 'concrete' means real and specific, and it is also the building material made of cement, sand, gravel and water.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: flour/flower, pair/pear, knight/night, peace/piece, weather/whether, stationary/stationery.
Homonyms have the same spelling and sound but different meanings: bat (cricket bat / flying animal), bank (money bank / river bank), bark (a dog's bark / a tree's bark).
Literal meaning is the plain meaning of the words; figurative meaning is a special or imaginative meaning. 'A piece of cake' literally is cake, but figuratively means 'very easy'.

example.q: Think it through: 'Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school!' Explain the pun.
steps: Find the word or phrase with two meanings: 'high school'.
Meaning 1: a level of school for older students.
Meaning 2: a school that is high up, so you would need a ladder.
The joke works because both meanings fit at once.
example.answer: 'High school' means a senior school and also, jokingly, a school that is high up, which is why she needs a ladder.

learn.reallife: Newspaper headlines, shop names and greeting cards love puns, like a tailor's shop called 'Sew Good' (it sounds like 'so good'). Spotting them makes reading more fun.

items.text: Dadi bought a kilo of wheat ___ to make rotis.
I don't know ___ it will rain today.
May I have a ___ of the birthday cake?
From the hotel window we could ___ the waves at Marina Beach.
The ___ of our school spoke at the assembly.

quiz.explain: Flour and flower sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.
steps: Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning.
'Flour' and 'flower' sound the same; big–large are synonyms and hot–cold antonyms.
Answer: flour – flower
quiz.mistake: Confuses homophones with synonyms or antonyms

quiz.q: 'The dog's bark woke me' and 'The tree's bark is rough.' Here 'bark' is a ___.
quiz.explain: The same word, spelt and said the same way, has two different meanings. That is a homonym.
steps: 'Bark' is spelt and said the same way in both sentences but means two things.
A word like that is a homonym.
Answer: homonym
quiz.mistake: Calls it a homophone, but homophones are spelt differently

quiz.q: Why is this a pun? 'I tried to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.'
options: 'Dough' means bread mixture and is also slang for money
quiz.explain: A baker makes dough (the mixture), and 'dough' is also an informal word for money. Both meanings work together.
steps: A pun plays on two meanings of one word.
'Dough' is the bread mixture a baker makes and also slang for money.
Answer: 'Dough' means bread mixture and is also slang for money
quiz.mistake: Looks for rhyme or exaggeration instead of a double meaning

quiz.q: In 'Give me a concrete example', the word 'concrete' means ___.
quiz.explain: Here 'concrete' is used figuratively to mean definite and real, not the building material.
steps: In 'a concrete example', concrete is used figuratively, not as cement.
It means real and specific.
Answer: real and specific
quiz.mistake: Uses the building-material meaning in the wrong context

quiz.q: Choose the correct word: The bus was ___ at the red signal.
quiz.explain: 'Stationary' means not moving. 'Stationery' means paper, pens and other writing materials.
steps: 'Stationary' means not moving; 'stationery' means paper and pens.
A bus stopped at a signal is not moving.
Answer: stationary
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two homophones stationary and stationery

options: Every child has the right to education.
quiz.explain: In 'Your answer is right', right means correct. The others mean a direction, a fair claim, or a side.
steps: 'Right' has several meanings: a direction, a fair claim, a side, or correct.
In 'Your answer is right', it means correct.
Answer: Your answer is right.
quiz.mistake: Does not use context to pick the meaning of a homonym

quiz.q: Which word is a homophone of 'knight'?
quiz.explain: The 'k' in knight is silent, so knight and night sound the same.
steps: The 'k' in 'knight' is silent.
So 'knight' sounds the same as 'night'.
Answer: night
quiz.mistake: Matches the spelling 'kn' instead of the sound

quiz.q: Ravi said, 'This maths homework is a piece of cake.' He means it is ___.
quiz.explain: 'A piece of cake' is an idiom meaning something very easy.
steps: 'A piece of cake' is an idiom.
It means something very easy.
Answer: very easy

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: Someone said 'I bought flour' and I pictured a rose! Explain homophones and puns to me.
teach.praise: Oh! Flour and flower sound the same but mean different things, and a pun jokes with those double meanings!
teach.nudge: Do flour and flower sound different? Are they spelt the same? How does a joke use that?

revise.summary: A pun plays on a word with two meanings or on words that sound alike, like the title 'A Concrete Example'. We also learn homophones, homonyms, and literal versus figurative meaning.
focus: Explain how a pun works using both meanings.
Use context to pick the right meaning or spelling.
remember: Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: flour/flower, pair/pear, knight/night, stationary/stationery.
Homonyms have the same spelling and sound but different meanings: bat, bank, bark.
'Concrete' means real and specific, and is also a building material.
traps: A homophone is spelt differently; same spelling and sound with two meanings is a homonym.
Don't mix up 'stationary' (not moving) and 'stationery' (paper, pens).
Don't take a figurative phrase literally: 'a piece of cake' means very easy.
